newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Anglo-Irish summit unlikely to hasten IRA truce.
newsitem.headline: Anglo-Irish summit unlikely to hasten IRA truce.

text.p: Hopes of an IRA guerrilla truce by Christmas appear to have been dimmed by British Prime Minister John Major's battle for political survival, Irish officials said on Sunday.
They said Major was unlikely to yield to pressure for concessions towards the IRA's Sinn Fein political wing when he meets Irish Prime Minister John Bruton in London on Monday.
Major appeared to confirm this view on Sunday, saying he would not accept a "phoney" IRA ceasfire just to secure a place for Sinn Fein at all-party Northern Irish peace talks.
Major told a BBC television interviewer he was not optimistic about the chances of a new IRA ceasefire, but said he could not rule one out. "I am not interested in a phoney ceasefire," he said.

Major's one-seat parliamentary majority vanished on Friday when a disaffected member of his Conservative party said he would no longer automatically vote with the government in a row over the closure of a hospital emergency ward.
"Major's hanging in by his fingernails, or by a finger nail. He's wobbling badly. It's hard to see how he can do anything for anyone at present," said one senior Irish official.

They said Major was also heavily dependent on the continued support of Northern Ireland's nine Unionist legislators, who want the province to stay British and fear Major is pandering to Sinn Fein to get all parties represented at the peace talks.

The Irish government is worried that failure to build on months of mediation work by peace-broker John Hume could be dashed unless Major eases the terms under which Sinn Fein could join other Northern Ireland parties at Belfast peace talks.

The Irish Republican Army, which seeks to end British rule of Northern Ireland and reunite the province with the Irish republic, has not carried out any attack since it bombed Britain's army base in the province on October 7.

Security sources fear deadlock over the talks' terms could lead to a new round of IRA attacks in Britain, Northern Ireland and elsewhere which could draw their Loyalist, pro-British rival guerrillas back into war after a two-year truce.

"These are dangerous times and this is a last-gasp effort. If there isn't an IRA truce in place before long God knows how long it will be before we can start talking about it again," said another Irish official.

At issue is how long it would take Sinn Fein to join the Belfast peace talks if the guerrillas called the truce that the province's 1.5 million ordinary people hope for. Sinn Fein says an IRA truce should give it immediate entry to the talks.

Northern Ireland minister Michael Ancram also insisted in a British newspaper interview on Sunday that the IRA, which ended a 17-month truce in February, would have to prove to Britain's satisfaction that a new truce was not a tactical ploy.

He said the IRA would have to end targetting and surveillance of potential victims and end "punishment beatings" of dissident or wayward supporters in the 40 percent Catholic minority, from which Sinn Fein draws support.

"It all depends on the IRA's actions and words. If their actions are not totally consistent with their words over a ceasefire, then obviously it would be a much longer period of trying to assess whether the ceasefire is genuine," Ancram said.
